claims.text: A domain model puts each business rule, as methods, in the class whose data the rule is about, so those methods become the way to change that data.
claims.source_hint: glossary domain-model; .NET microservices guide: Design a microservice domain model (rich domain model, behavior in entities)

claims.text: At stage-2 Order.Cancel() throws OrderStatusException with code already-cancelled when Status is cancelled, with code already-shipped when Status is shipped, and otherwise sets Status to cancelled.

At stage-2 CancelOrderAsync finds the order (KeyNotFoundException if missing), calls order.Cancel(), then notifier.Send, then SaveChangesAsync; its body has no status check or comparison with shipped (only the comment mentions it); at stage-1 it saved before sending.
If order.Cancel() throws, CancelOrderAsync stops before notifier.Send and SaveChangesAsync, so nothing about the refused cancel is written.
claims.source_hint: C# docs: exceptions (an unhandled exception ends the method); OrderService.cs:45-47 @ stage-2

claims.text: OrderStatusException is declared in DonHang.Domain (OrderStatusException.cs), carries OrderId and Code, derives from Exception, and names no HTTP status; DonHang.Domain.csproj has no project or package reference.
ExceptionHandlingMiddleware in DonHang.Api catches OrderStatusException and writes a 409 problem whose type is https://donhang.local/problems/ followed by ex.Code, so each code gets its own type.
At stage-2 PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel for a shipped order answers 409 with a type ending in already-shipped (after the owner check passes).

Moving a rule into Order pays off when several use cases change the same data (each calls the method and gets the check); for data whose only rule is a simple check on an incoming value, methods would only set a value.

At stage-2 Product has only public auto-properties and no methods; its price must be above zero, kept by UpdateProductPriceRequest's [Range(1, int.MaxValue)] (Dtos.cs:10) and CHECK (price_vnd > 0) in db/schema.sql.

At stage-2 QueuedNotifier.Send only adds a pending notifications row to the same scoped DonHangDbContext as the order, so the single SaveChangesAsync writes the order and the job together; hence Send comes before the save.
The status code is a decision of the web side; DonHang.Domain should only say which rule was broken.
Order.Cancel() only changes Status in memory; saving is IOrderRepository.SaveChangesAsync called by OrderService; Order has no repository or DbContext member.

At stage-2, git grep -n "throw new OrderStatusException" -- "DonHang.*/*.cs" prints 7 lines, all in DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs (MarkPaid, Cancel, Ship); git grep -n "OrderStatusException" -- "DonHang.Api/*.cs" prints 2: OrdersController.cs:70 (comment) and ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs:36 (catch).
claims.source_hint: verified with git grep on tag stage-2 in examples/don-hang

Any caller of Order.Cancel(), not only ExceptionHandlingMiddleware, can catch OrderStatusException and read its Code property.
